title: Manage ATTENTION with effective User Interface (UI) Design
section: 12. Web Design School - Create a Website that People Love
summary: UI design directs where users look. Five principles: visual hierarchy, layout, alignment, white space, and designing for the target audience. Each is illustrated with real-site examples and simple rules of thumb.

concepts.heading: 1. Hierarchy
points: Eyes go first to what is bigger, bolder and higher in contrast. Ranking information by importance lets people skim instead of reading everything.
If all text has equal weight (as in a plain invitation paragraph), the reader must read it all to find the key facts. With hierarchy, the key facts (whose event, where, when) come first.

Colour: bright, high-contrast colours signal importance; muted or grey tones signal less importance. An ecommerce example keeps a neutral grey/white palette and uses a green accent to pull attention to the add-to-bag action.

Size: the largest elements get noticed first. A crypto exchange landing page makes its headline biggest, then the email field and Get started button, because capturing the visitor's email is the goal.
(Extra) In CSS terms, hierarchy comes from font-size, font-weight, colour, contrast and spacing.

concepts.heading: 2. Layout
points: A wall of uniform text is dull. Mix text blocks with images and vary shapes, sizes and emphasis to keep interest.
Chop content into smaller pieces so visitors absorb more of the page (a grammar tool site is the positive example, an encyclopedia page the negative one).
Line length: aim for about 40-60 characters per line. Longer lines make the eye lose its track; shorter ones feel choppy.
(Extra) In CSS, limit line length with max-width in ch units, for example max-width: 60ch.

concepts.heading: 3. Alignment
points: Elements should share clear starting edges. A centred title above left-aligned body text looks mismatched; giving both the same left edge looks deliberate.
Reduce the number of distinct alignment lines in a design. Draw an imaginary line through the start of each item and merge lines where possible.
Better alignment alone, with no change to colour or fonts, makes a design look more professional.

concepts.heading: 4. White space
points: White space is the empty area around text and elements. Luxury shops use it to signal quality, while crowded displays suggest a discount store.
The same applies to digital ads: stuffing a headphone ad with badges and prices looks cheap; spacing it out looks premium and minimalist.
(Extra) In CSS use padding, margin, gap and line-height to create it.

concepts.heading: 5. Know your audience
points: Style rules depend on who the site is for. A very severe black-and-white children's concert poster fails, while a colourful playful one fits.
Be flexible: teenagers buying clothes, crypto traders and a medical site each need a different visual style.
A bolder, messier style is fine when it suits the audience.

pitfalls: Giving every element the same visual weight.
Very long text lines and walls of text.
Mixing centre and left alignment without reason, or having many different alignment lines.
Cramming content together with no breathing room.
Applying one style regardless of audience.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'UI principles': blurb on hierarchy, alignment and white space. Tasks: 1) make the call-to-action the most prominent element; 2) limit paragraph width to 60ch; 3) align the title and body to one left edge; 4) add padding and margins to a cramped card grid; 5) restyle the page for a playful kids' audience.
Starter code idea: a cramped pricing page with centred and left-aligned text mixed and every element the same size.
Interactive demo idea: sliders for max-width, padding and font-size with a live 'characters per line' counter and an eye-path heat overlay.
